Keeper
KEEP-ur
n. (one who guards, tends, or has charge of; rendering Hebrew shamar participle, Greek phylax, oikouros)
English agent-noun from keep. The Hebrew verb behind it, shamar, is the word used of Adam in the garden (to dress it and to keep it) and of God keeping Israel — the same duty, at two scales.

Biblical Definition

A keeper is one charged with guarding what is not finally his own, and Scripture's first use of the word is a question thrown at God in bad faith: “And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?” (Genesis 4:9). Cain's sneer has become a proverb, generally quoted as though the answer were obvious; the text leaves it unanswered because the whole subsequent Bible is the answer. The word had already been used two verses earlier of Abel's occupation — “Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground” (Genesis 4:2) — so Cain is throwing his murdered brother's own job title back at God. Against that stands the Psalter's most concentrated use of the root, where the same verb appears six times in eight verses: “he that keepeth thee will not slumber” and “The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand” (Psalm 121:3, 5). The pilgrim going up to Jerusalem is told that his safety is not vigilance but a Keeper who does not sleep — a pointed contrast with Baal, of whom Elijah suggested he might be sleeping and need awakening. The office runs down through Scripture: keepers of the door, of the wardrobe, of the prison, of the vineyard, and keepers at home.

Webster 1828 Definition

One charged with guarding what is not his own. Cain's sneer — Am I my brother's keeper? — is left unanswered because the rest of Scripture answers it; Psalm 121 says the LORD is thy keeper and does not slumber.

expand to see more

KEEPER, n. One who keeps; one that holds or has possession of any thing.

2. One who retains in custody; one who has the care of a prison and the custody of prisoners.

3. One who has the care, custody or superintendence of any thing; as the keeper of the great seal; a gamekeeper.

4. One who has the care of flocks or herds; a shepherd. Abel was a keeper of sheep. Gen. 4.

5. A protector; a guardian; as, the Lord is thy keeper. Ps. 121.

Key Scripture

Genesis 4:9 — "And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?"

Psalm 121:5 — "The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand."

Psalm 121:3 — "He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber."

Genesis 4:2 — "And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground."

Modern Corruption

Cain's question is quoted approvingly as a defence of privacy and non-interference — and inside the church, as a reason not to pursue an erring brother, which is the one use Scripture most directly forbids.

expand to see more

“Am I my brother's keeper?” is one of the few Bible verses everyone can quote and one of the few whose speaker is a murderer covering his tracks. It is used now to close conversations: what my neighbour does is his own affair, what I do is mine, and the man who interferes is presumptuous. Scripture's answer, given at length rather than in a sentence, is yes. Every man is his brother's keeper — Leviticus 19:17 requires rebuking a neighbour rather than hating him in the heart, Galatians 6:1 charges the spiritual with restoring the overtaken, and James ends by promising that turning a sinner from the error of his way saves a soul from death. The church's practice of discipline is nothing more than the corporate form of that duty, and its collapse in most congregations is Cain's question adopted as policy.

There is a real counterfeit that has given the objection its force, and it should be named. Keeping a brother is not surveillance, and Scripture puts hard limits on it: Paul forbids suffering as a busybody in other men's matters (1 Peter 4:15), commands that a man study to be quiet and do his own business (1 Thessalonians 4:11), and lays down a procedure in Matthew 18 that begins privately, between two, before anything becomes public. Churches that have inverted this — making every fault a congregational matter, or a leader's knowledge of every household's affairs a mark of care — have not been more faithful than Cain, only differently unfaithful. The keeper of a flock protects it; he does not audit it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shamar (to keep, guard, watch over) — used of Adam keeping the garden, Abel keeping sheep, and the LORD keeping Israel; Greek phylax (a guard) and oikouros (a keeper at home).

expand to see more

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, observe; the verb repeated six times in Psalm 121 and used of Adam in Genesis 2:15.

Hebrew ro'eh / ro'eh tson — a keeper of sheep, shepherd; Abel's occupation in Genesis 4:2.

Greek phylasso (G5442) — to guard, keep watch; used of keeping the commandments and of God keeping the believer.

Greek phylax (G5441) — a guard, keeper; used of the prison keepers in Acts 5:23 and 12:6.

Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, watch over, preserve; the verb in John 17:11-12, where Christ keeps those given Him.

Usage

"“Am I my brother's keeper?” — a murderer's evasion, now quoted as a principle."

"“The LORD is thy keeper” — the pilgrim's safety is a Keeper, not his own vigilance."

"“He that keepeth thee will not slumber” — a pointed contrast with the gods who need waking."
